correctness.rationale: For a Euclidean full-dimensional polytope, the center locus for embedded radius-r balls is exactly the convex intersection of facet halfspaces shifted inward by r. Hausdorff loss is a maximum of point-to-convex-opening distances at original vertices. Their distances to the eroded polytope are bounded below by r times a feasible pointed-cone minimum norm lambda_v. The minimizer satisfies every nonincident offset constraint for sufficiently small r because there is strict nonincident facet slack, proving local equality simultaneously at all finitely many vertices. In a planar wedge lambda=csc(theta/2); angle sum gives sec(pi/n)-1 for every admissible radius. Regular n-gons have a homothetic eroded polygon, so support functions prove equality for all r, including inradius. Inverting the lower bound gives explicit angle rigidity; rhombus perturbations prove sharp linear order. Real-quantified statements rely on these steps, not floating-point tests. Supplementary verifier successfully checked 220 randomized polygons at two radii, 112 regular-polygon and 16 rectangle cases.

originality.rationale: Cappello provides the erosion/union-of-balls definitions and a general point-to-opening distance identity, but proves C1alpha smoothness equivalences rather than polytope vertex-cone coefficients or sharp polygon side-count inequalities. Heppes (1963) explicitly describes polygonal disk opening as corner rounding, so that premise is credited, but develops area/perimeter problems without the Hausdorff coefficient, fixed-n sharp inequality, equality and angle-stability conclusions. Both relevant published mathematical records checked in full concern distinct angle-related functionals (Pach-Tardos triangle roundness and local random pair-distance coefficients). Targeted aliases and dominant-parameter searches in published published-finding corpus records and literature did not identify equivalent or stronger direct coverage. Historical priority remains provisional because older morphology sources may contain an unlocated equivalent. The independent proof and quantitative all-radius angular rigidity, not the operation itself, form the claim.

value.rationale: Cappello 2026 directly motivates quantitative approximation of convex bodies by unions of contained balls. For nonsmooth shapes the singular vertex obstruction is a mathematically natural feature. Beyond the classical qualitative statement that corners are rounded, the theorem gives a computable high-dimensional tangent-cone coefficient for each polytope, a sharp universal lower bound across every planar n-gon and every admissible radius, its exact equality class locally and regular extremizers globally, plus a quantitative angle-rigidity modulus with optimal linear order. These jointly settle a natural sharp minimax and stability problem for fixed polygonal facet budget. It does not claim new morphological definitions or smooth-body theorems.
